opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that LLM inference, especially the decode phase, is fundamentally limited by memory bandwidth and by how efficiently you move data, not by raw compute. On a conventional GPU, you execute a model as a sequence of kernels. Each kernel reads its inputs from high-bandwidth memory, does some work, and writes results back out, and then the next kernel picks them up again. For a transformer, that means a lot of round trips to off-chip memory and a lot of kernel launch overhead, and you end up leaving much of the hardware's potential on the table.

With a reconfigurable dataflow architecture, which is what we've built at SambaNova, you take the computation graph of the model and map it spatially onto the chip. Instead of running one operator at a time, you fuse a whole sequence of operators, potentially an entire decoder layer or more, into a single pipeline. Data streams from one stage to the next through on-chip memory and the interconnect without going back out to HBM. That aggressive operator fusion and pipelining is really where the efficiency comes from. You get much higher utilization of both compute and bandwidth, and you can generate tokens much faster.

The second piece is the memory hierarchy. Large models, and especially the trend toward serving many models or mixtures of experts, put pressure on capacity as well as bandwidth. We designed a three-tier memory system: large on-chip SRAM distributed across the fabric, HBM for bandwidth, and a large pool of DDR for capacity. That lets you keep many models, or many experts, resident on a single node and switch between them very quickly. That matters a lot for things like agentic workflows, where you might chain together many different specialized models, or for composition-of-experts approaches.

And then the reconfigurability itself is important because the field is moving so fast. Model architectures keep changing: new attention variants, state space models, different MoE routing schemes. A fixed-function accelerator risks being obsolete by the time it's built. A reconfigurable dataflow fabric lets the compiler adapt the mapping to whatever the new model looks like, while still getting the efficiency benefits of a spatial, specialized execution. So you get something close to custom-hardware performance, with the flexibility of software. That combination is why I think dataflow is such a natural fit for where inference is heading.

r001.rationale: The response says LLM decode is fundamentally limited by memory bandwidth and describes repeated transfers to and from HBM.

r002.rationale: It describes streaming fused operators through on-chip memory and the interconnect without returning to HBM, reducing off-chip round trips.

r003.rationale: It describes spatial mapping onto a chip and says a decoder layer or more may be fused, but does not say an entire decoder is mapped across multiple accelerator chips.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. The short answer is that large language model inference is fundamentally a data movement problem, not a compute problem, and reconfigurable dataflow is an architecture organized around data movement rather than around instructions.

Let me unpack that a bit. If you look at what happens during inference, particularly in the decode phase where you're generating tokens one at a time, you're taking a relatively small amount of activation data and streaming it through an enormous set of weights. The arithmetic intensity is low. For every weight you pull from memory, you do very little work with it. So on a conventional GPU, you end up memory-bandwidth bound. The compute units sit idle waiting for data to arrive from HBM, and your utilization numbers are often in the single digits or low teens.

A reconfigurable dataflow architecture attacks that from a different direction. Instead of a sea of cores that fetch instructions and fetch operands from a memory hierarchy, you have an array of compute units and memory units connected by a programmable interconnect. You take the computation graph of the model, the sequence of matrix multiplies, the attention, the normalization, the activation functions, and you map it spatially onto the chip. Each stage of the pipeline lives in a particular region of the fabric, and data flows directly from one stage to the next through the on-chip network. You're not writing intermediate results back to off-chip memory and reading them again. That's where most of the bandwidth gets wasted in a kernel-by-kernel execution model.

There are a few consequences of that which matter specifically for LLMs. The first is that you can fuse operations very aggressively, essentially the whole transformer layer, without the compiler having to fight the hardware. On a GPU, kernel fusion is something you do by hand with a lot of effort. On a dataflow machine it's the natural mode of execution. The second is that you can hold a lot of state on chip. These architectures tend to have large amounts of distributed SRAM, hundreds of megabytes, so things like the KV cache for attention or the weights of a layer can stay resident while you stream through them. The third, and this is the one I find most interesting right now, is that you can be flexible about where the weights live. We've been looking at three-tier memory systems, SRAM on chip, HBM, and then DDR behind that, and a dataflow architecture lets you pipeline across those tiers so that the bandwidth of each level is being used concurrently rather than serially. That becomes important when you want to serve very large models, or many models, on a single system without being limited by how much HBM you can attach to a package.

The last thing I'd say is that the workload itself is changing. We're seeing mixture-of-experts models, agentic workloads where you're switching between models, speculative decoding, longer contexts. All of those stress the system in ways that reward the ability to reconfigure how data moves rather than just adding more FLOPs. The flexibility of the architecture is a feature precisely because nobody knows exactly what the inference workload looks like two years from now.

r001.rationale: It says inference is memory-bandwidth bound on GPUs because weights streamed from HBM leave compute units waiting for data.

r002.rationale: It describes mapping computation across the fabric so intermediate results stay on chip instead of being written to and reread from off-chip memory.

r003.rationale: It says the model computation graph is mapped spatially onto a chip, but does not say an entire decoder is mapped across multiple accelerator chips.

astra-6.text:
The key is that large language model inference is as much about moving data as it is about doing arithmetic. You need to get the weights and the intermediate results to the compute units efficiently, and that balance changes depending on how you’re running the model.

With a reconfigurable dataflow architecture, we can organize the hardware around the computation. We map operations onto compute resources and configure the paths between them so that data flows directly from one operation to the next. That gives us opportunities to keep intermediate results on chip and avoid repeatedly writing them out to memory and reading them back.

For language models, that’s particularly useful because you have different execution patterns. Processing the input prompt exposes a lot of parallelism, while generating tokens one at a time can be much more constrained by memory bandwidth. Reconfigurability lets us adapt how we use the compute and memory resources to those different demands.

So the attraction is efficiency through specialization, while retaining the flexibility to support models as they evolve. You’re tailoring the execution to the model without having to build a new chip for every model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses memory bandwidth generally, but does not identify HBM bandwidth as a fundamental bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It describes keeping intermediate results on chip and avoiding repeated memory reads and writes, but does not identify minimizing transfers over HBM as the objective.

r003.rationale: It describes mapping operations onto compute resources, but does not say an entire decoder can be spatially mapped across multiple accelerator chips.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you look at large language model inference, you have to think about both computation and moving data. You can have a tremendous amount of arithmetic capability, but if you can’t keep it supplied with data, you’re not going to get the performance you want.

A reconfigurable dataflow architecture lets us organize the hardware around the way data moves through the model. We can configure compute units for different operations, place intermediate results in on-chip memory, and stream those results directly to the next operation. That reduces the need to repeatedly go back to external memory, which costs both time and energy.

And inference has different phases. Processing the prompt gives you a lot of parallel computation, while generating tokens one at a time puts much more pressure on memory bandwidth and latency. Reconfigurability gives us flexibility in how we map those workloads onto the machine. So the opportunity is to get efficient execution across those different phases, while retaining the ability to adapt as models change.

r001.rationale: The response discusses memory bandwidth and external memory generally, but does not identify HBM bandwidth as a fundamental bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says on-chip intermediate results reduce repeated trips to external memory, but does not specify minimizing data transfers over HBM.

r003.rationale: It describes mapping workloads onto a reconfigurable machine, but does not say an entire decoder can be spatially mapped across multiple accelerator chips.
